introduction: Today the Church keeps the World Day of the Poor. In the Gospel, a master entrusts his servants with his wealth and later asks what they have done with it. The first reading praises a woman whose strength and wisdom are shown in her work and in her open hands to the poor. Every gift we have comes from God, and is given to be used for others. As we gather, let us thank God for his gifts and ask for the courage to invest them in love.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Everything we have is God's gift. With grateful hearts, let us bring before him the needs of the Church and of the world.
intentions: For the Church: that she may always be poor in spirit and rich in love, a home where the poor feel welcome. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who live in poverty, hunger or homelessness: that they may receive help with dignity and find friends, not only benefactors, among us. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel they have little to offer: that they may discover the gifts God has given them and use them without fear. Let us pray to the Lord.
For women and mothers who serve their families and communities quietly: that God may bless their work and that it may be honoured. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our parish: that we may each use our time, abilities and goods to build up the Body of Christ and serve those in need. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Generous Father, every good gift comes from you. Accept our prayers, and make us faithful stewards of all you have entrusted to us, so that we may enter into the joy of our Lord. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The servant who was afraid
reflection.body:
A talent was an enormous sum, the wages of many years of work. In the parable, a man going on a journey entrusts his property to three servants, "to each according to his own ability." Two of them trade and double what they were given. The third digs a hole and buries his share. When the master returns, the first two hear the words every disciple longs for: "Well done, good and faithful servant... Enter into the joy of your lord."

What went wrong with the third servant? He did not steal or waste the money. He simply did nothing with it, and he tells us why: "I knew you that you are a hard man... I was afraid." His failure began with a false image of his master. Because he saw the master as harsh, he was afraid, and fear made him bury what he had been given.

Many of us carry a similar image of God: a stern examiner waiting for us to fail. But the master in the parable is extravagantly generous. He trusts his servants with his wealth and then, when they are faithful, invites them to share his joy. Where we see God as a hard master, we play safe and bury our gifts. Where we know him as a loving Father, we can take risks for love.

The first reading offers a portrait of a woman who did not bury her talents. She works with eager hands, her husband trusts her, and "she opens her arms to the poor; yes, she extends her hands to the needy." Her greatness is not charm or beauty, which fade, but her reverence for the Lord, which shows itself in work and in generosity.

On this World Day of the Poor, the parable presses close. Our talents are not only abilities; they are time, money, education, faith, a listening ear. None of it was given to be hidden. Paul tells us we are children of the light, not of the night. Let us live in that light, using what we have received, so that one day we too may hear: "Well done."
